title: Reformulating Neural Operators in $d+1$ Dimensions for Embedding Evolution
claim: Operators on d-dimensional functions can be recast as one operator in d+1 dimensions, adding an auxiliary axis that evolves the lifted embedding.
layout: 3 columns, left-to-right; lift/recover arrows, 1D operator above (d+1)D operator
description: The figure has three columns. The left column shows an input function a(x) as a 1D curve on x–y axes. A thick blue arrow labeled Lifting points down to a 3D plot of v_t(x,p), where the curve is copied along a new p axis. The right column mirrors this. A 3D surface v_{t+1}(x,p) goes up through a thick arrow labeled Recovering to the 1D output u(x). The center column contrasts two operators. The top shows a blue '1D Operator' box with an 'Evolution x' arrow. The bottom shows a red 3D box labeled '(1+1)D Neural Operator' with two arrows, 'Evolution x' and a dashed 'Evolution p'. Blue marks the 1D case and red marks the extended case, so the eye goes to the red box. Bold titles label each center row.
caption: Different $d$-dimensional operators can be parameterized by the $(d+1)$-dimensional Neural Operator which flexibly represents the evolution on both $x$ and $p$.
abstract: Neural Operators (NOs) are powerful architectures for learning mappings between function spaces. While most advances focus on refining kernel parameterizations over the $d$-dimensional physical domain, the evolution of lifted embeddings remains underexplored, which often drives models toward computationally expensive embedding-scaling designs to improve approximation. In this paper, we introduce an auxiliary function dimension that models embedding evolution in operator form, thereby reformulating the NO pipeline in $d+1$ dimensions. We instantiate this framework via Fourier-based operators acting jointly on the physical and auxiliary domains, yielding a basis-diversified auxiliary evolution module as an alternative to brute-force embedding scaling. Across more than ten increasingly challenging benchmarks, ranging from the 1D heat equation to the highly nonlinear 3D Rayleigh-Taylor instability, our model consistently achieves the lowest relative $L_2$ error among the evaluated baselines. Crucially, this advantage is empirically supported by (1) controlled budget-aware comparisons against scaled and ablated baselines; (2) robustness under mixed-resolution training and super-resolution inference; and (3) zero-shot generalization to unseen temporal regimes. In addition, we present a broader set of design choices for lifting and recovery operators, demonstrating their impact on our model's predictive performance.
